data.title: Big Tech's compliance with EU market rules is performative, consumer group says
data.description:
Big Tech has earned a finger-wagging from the European Consumer Organisation (BEUC), which says the industry's compliance with the EU's Digital Markets Act (DMA) still leaves consumers short of meaningful choice.

BEUC said: "Big Tech companies Alphabet, Amazon, Apple, ByteDance, Meta and Microsoft (so-called 'gatekeepers') still likely breach the EU's Digital Markets Act (DMA) far too often for consumers to reap the full benefits of real choice over their digital services and products."

The European Commission designated the six companies as gatekeepers in 2023, imposing obligations on specified core platform services such as search engines, messaging services, and app stores. The DMA aims to make digital markets fairer and more open to competition.

The devil is in the details. In the years since, the EC has lined up Amazon and Microsoft's cloud businesses for gatekeeper status. In March 2025, the Commission issued preliminary findings against Alphabet over Search and Google Play, while separately specifying measures Apple had to take to meet its interoperability obligations. In 2024, Microsoft's browser rivals argued that Edge should also be covered by the DMA's gatekeeper obligations, and so on.

BEUC is a fan of the act – it published a report on its consumer benefits in 2025 – but is less impressed with industry's implementation. Its latest analysis draws together evidence of potential breaches submitted to the Commission between June 2025 and June 2026.

In the case of Microsoft, BEUC stated that the company used "behavioural techniques" and "non-neutral interfaces" to elicit consent from users for data sharing across services – emphasizing benefits, while not explaining why a user might want to decline. The Windows behemoth is also accused of making it tricky to change defaults and stop behavior such as apps opening links in Edge or using Bing as a search engine.

"Microsoft also regularly prompts users who have selected an alternative browser or search engine to switch to Edge or Bing using increasingly subliminal techniques, such as prompts coming from the device manufacturer, which undermine effective compliance with the DMA," BEUC said.

Then there's Google, which was fined €890 million in July for favoring its own services in Search and restricting developers' ability to direct Play Store users to alternative purchasing channels. As with Microsoft, BEUC expressed concerns about the non-neutral language Google used to obtain user consent, as well as how it allegedly made it difficult to change default settings or uninstall gatekeeper applications.

The alleged behavior of Apple, ByteDance, Amazon, and Meta was also highlighted, with examples including Apple's restrictions on alternative app distribution and Amazon using interface design techniques to nudge users into handing over their data.

Apple announced new terms for developers earlier this year in response to its App Store dispute with the European Commission, but BEUC said it was "concerned that the new terms do not resolve fundamental non-compliance issues."

Google did not respond to requests for comment from The Register. A Microsoft spokesperson told us: "We are continuing to engage with the Commission and industry at large to ensure Microsoft's designated platforms comply fully with the DMA."

An Amazon spokesperson told The Register “Our consent experience is clear and gives customers informed choice about how their personal information is used across Amazon services. We see that in practice.

“A seller that uses Amazon Stores in the EU can offer the same products on any third-party online marketplace or its own direct to customer website at any price, without affecting their eligibility to be highlighted as the Featured Offer. This is set out clearly in our DMA Compliance Report.”

BEUC director general Agustín Reyna said: "The era of cosmetic compliance must end. It is high time the Commission holds gatekeepers to account and imposes dissuasive penalties in all cases where they bypass the DMA's rules."

The report has been shared with the Commission. Whether BEUC's allegations lead to further findings of non-compliance or penalties is now a matter for the regulator. ®

data.title: Nvidia adds possible hack to list of very bad things under investigation
data.description:
Finding a new CEO is just one of their problems. Nvidia is investigating an alleged breach following claims by ransomware group The Gentlemen's affiliates that they hacked the AI giant and stole sensitive information.

The embattled chipmaker told The Register's that it was investigating a possible third-party data breach. “We have found no indication that Nvidia systems or networks were affected,” a spokesperson said. “We continue to monitor the situation." 

The ransomware gang’s data-leak site, shared on social media and seen by The Register, doesn’t show any stolen files or indicate what information the group claims to have stolen. Nvidia first appeared on the criminals’ blog on Wednesday, with The Gentlemen promising “DATA INFO - SOON.” 

The post also included a countdown, ending November 28.

While we can’t verify the criminals’ claims, the group, which emerged in mid-2025, is one of the most prolific ransomware-as-a-service operations. Its affiliates claimed more than 320 victims as of April, with the majority of these alleged ransomware infections (240) occurring in the first half of 2026. 

The actual count, however, is likely much higher. Check Point researchers accessed an affiliate’s live command-and-control server during an incident response case earlier this year. The server contained victim telemetry that revealed more than 1,570 victims, mostly located in the US, and primarily corporate and organizational environments.

According to an operational technology (OT) threat report from Trellix published on Wednesday, industrial ransomware claims jumped nearly 51 percent - to about 1,500 posts- compared to last quarter, and The Gentlemen’s affiliates were the most prolific claim posters during this time period. They accounted for about 16 percent of all posts.

In February 2022, an Nvidia data breach exposed employees’ credentials and proprietary code. Extortion crew Lapsus$ claimed to be responsible for that intrusion and data theft.®

data.title: XXRI-OS explores the lowest end of the Linux desktop
data.description:
New Linux distros seem to appear daily, but far too few distinguish themselves by being smaller and simpler.

XXRI OS is a fairly new desktop Linux distro. It has a snazzy-looking website, complete with an amusing URL, and along similar lines, its GitHub page has a very heavily formatted README. Nonetheless, this is not another over-complex opinionated slopfest of an OS with built-in AI, bizarre keystrokes, and several proprietary components. It's almost the reverse.

The main download is just 287.4 MB, and that's the full distro, not a minimalist installer that fetches most of the OS over your internet connection. We installed it in a VirtualBox VM. It took 675 MB of disk space, and in the graphical desktop, when we opened a terminal window, it reported just 75 MB of RAM in use with the desktop and terminal running. We are restraining ourselves hard when we say that those are unusually low numbers for the 2020s. We would expect most cut-down lightweight Linux distros to use around five to 10 times as much disk space or memory.

The current release of XXRI-OS is version 2.7. XXRI OS 1.0 came out in May 2025, making this a young project with five published releases already behind it. It also has much deeper roots: it is based on the existing and much older Tiny Core Linux. The Reg FOSS desk last looked at Tiny Core Linux 15 back in March 2024 and the project is still going strong: the latest version is version 17.1.

Tiny Core Linux is a marvel, but there are prices to pay for somehow getting a graphical Linux desktop into a 23 MB download. It runs from RAM and uses its own extension-based package system, which can make adding components and managing updates unfamiliar territory. XXRI OS takes TCL and turns it into a slightly more conventional desktop.

It installs to disk in the usual way, and it includes the core functions that most people would expect from their OS in 2026. It has a file manager, a text editor, a media player, a simple app store for adding further components, and a settings app including an update manager. It even includes its own web browser, and there are both x86-32 and x86-64 variants.

The desktop layout has a floating dock at bottom center, and the icons are unlabelled. To save you some guesswork, though, floating just to the left of the dock is an icon with a grid of dots, which is an app launcher. The icons in that do have text labels underneath, so you can learn which symbol denotes which function from here.

We plan to experiment more with this remarkable little OS and see how well it runs on the oldest, slowest boxes in the Irish Sea wing of Vulture Towers, but we like what we see so far. It's an impressive experiment in how low Linux can go and remain useful. While Tiny Core Linux goes down to Windows 95 levels of resource usage, XXRI OS has a more usable Windows 2000-level baseline. Over a quarter of a century later, that is nearly unbeatable. ®

data.title: Russian national accused of stalking San Francisco techie in plot against US defense-tech giant
data.description:
A Russian national is being held in custody after being arrested for allegedly spying on a US defense tech company in Palo Alto, shoulder-surfing employees, and dropping remote surveillance devices at their homes.

Igor D'iu was indicted after FBI agents surveilled his activities between June and October 2026, which they say were issued as "tasks" from what is thought to be Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB), according to an affidavit [PDF] signed by an FBI special agent.

After FBI agents secured a warrant to raid D'iu's temporary premises in October, they say that Telegram messages harvested from his seized devices confirmed investigators' findings and revealed that he was spying on an unnamed company. 

Court documents describe the company in question as a large technology and defense company with offices in Palo Alto, and media-reported links to the Russia-Ukraine war. 

While unconfirmed officially, the company has widely been reported as Palantir, which did not respond to our request for confirmation.

D'iu allegedly received instructions from Telegram contacts, whom he only suspected were representatives of the Russian government, weeks after entering the US illegally in July.

The indictment alleges he was ordered to surveil employees' homes, take photographs of their screens while working remotely at coffee shops, and permit his handlers to remotely access his laptop for the purpose of capturing data from nearby devices owned by the company’s employees.

In some cases, the filing alleges, D’iu was asked to leave a laptop outside one employee's apartment complex, all while allowing his Telegram handlers to remotely operate the device.

The first time, he was asked to leave the laptop for one hour while the handlers worked, and another time, he was told to drop it off in the middle of the night and only come back to collect it three hours later, the filing claims.

D'iu is also allegedly to have followed two female employees in his rented car, driving dangerously and violating multiple road laws to do so. 

One of the two employees was followed briefly, but D'iu followed another for nearly 30 miles, according to the affidavit signed by FBI special agent Winston Wong. 

D'iu was said to have followed the woman as she performed U-turns, illegal left turns, ran red lights, navigated via back and side streets, and through grocery store parking lots. 

The car following her only peeled away after the woman drove to the San Francisco Mission police station on the advice of a 911 call handler.

Questioned about the incident, which according to police reports caused the woman significant emotional distress, D'iu confirmed he was the driver but  claimed he was following her to ask her out on a date.

Inside recruitment

The affidavit did not detail the suspect's background beyond his alleged offenses in the US earlier this year, although it mentioned Russian intelligence's history of recruiting "criminal proxies, organized crime groups, and other disposable agents" to carry out operations.

According to the FBI's account, D'iu entered the US illegally – without relevant visas – in either June or July 2026. Travel records obtained on September 10 showed that his last recorded journey was from Istanbul to Mexico City. There was no record of him entering the US.

Investigators would later come to know that he travelled on that Istanbul-Mexico City flight on June 7, allegedly using a ticket provided to him by one of the three contacts from whom he received orders via Telegram.

A Facebook account, registered using a Mexican +528 number and D'iu's name, posted on June 30 asking for help getting "closer to New York," adding that "I'll pay as much as needed." The account replied to a response from someone who told him to contact a Mexico phone number on WhatsApp.

The filing claims the first mobile phone signals associated with D'iu's devices did not ping US towers until a month later, on July 31, suggesting he did not arrive in the US - specifically McAllen, Texas - until around that date. Telegram messages would also go on to confirm that he was allegedly helped across the border by an "Uzbek contact" in Mexico.

Records obtained from Google showed D'iu created a Google account in April. According to the affidavit, D'iu used it to search for the company's Wikipedia page on July 28, and on August 3, used Google's AI to devise a route around Texas that bypassed border checkpoints.

The FBI believes D'iu's "spying" began in mid-August, after he bought a laptop, a Wi-Fi device, a puck device, and an additional phone. At this point, the agency claims, he had received his first order to visit a coffee shop near the Palo Alto company’s office and snap employees' laptop screens before sending copies back to his handlers.

Three days later, D'iu was ordered to go back to a coffee shop and allow his Telegram contacts to remotely control the laptop and collect data from employee devices that were in range, claims the filing.

D'iu was paid $15,000 on three occasions between August 12 and October 6, according to the court documents. To verify the transaction, he was told to send a picture of a dollar bill's serial number to the Telegram contacts, along with a description of what he was wearing. A courier would then arrive, confirming the serial number and handing D'iu the cash.

The filing alleges he used this money to purchase the tech equipment, accommodation, and travel, including a rented silver 2026 Lexus RX 350 from a private owner in Los Angeles on August 22, which he is said to have driven back to San Francisco.

The same Lexus was captured on security footage outside the unnamed company's office on September 1, and over the following two days was implicated in the two instances of female employees being followed. 

Contacted by Palo Alto police on September 4, D'iu confirmed he was the driver who dangerously followed the female staffer for nearly 30 minutes, but claimed he knew nothing about the nearby businesses. D'iu would then claim he followed the woman because he thought she was beautiful and wanted to ask her out on a date, and denied following anyone else.

The affidavit goes on to allege that D'iu then traveled to Reno, Nevada, to lay low after his run-in with the police. He spent the time trying to reroute DHL deliveries from San Francisco to his hideout address, which US Customs would later intercept. 

These ended up containing fake IDs with the images the DoJ claims matched D'iu's, including Uzbek documents, a US passport whose number belonged to a New York woman, and a social security card registered to a "Hugo Landry Johns."

He traveled back to the Bay Area in late September, swapping his silver Lexus for a white 2016 Dodge Challenger, and received additional instructions from his handlers, including the order to leave a remote-controlled laptop outside the apartment complex, says the filing.

One Telegram contact named Ian Morales sent photos of at least four employees and their addresses, along with instructions for D'iu to dress as a food delivery worker and visit those locations, asking whoever answered to verify they lived there.

FBI agents executed a search warrant on October 8, seizing a cache of evidence, including what they listed as being:

  • The forged ID documents

  • Two Russian passports

  • $18,035 in cash

  • Two laptops

  • Two iPhones

  • Two T-Mobile SIM cards

  • Wi-Fi equipment

  • A notebook with 10 handwritten addresses supplied by Telegram contacts, along with times the suspect was supposed to attend those locations, at least five of which were for company employees’ homes

  • Profile packages for at least three employees, including: Names, personal information, education and employment histories, names of relatives, narrative histories, and assessments of leadership qualities, strengths, and weaknesses.

Suspicions and charges

Per the affidavit, D'iu was said to have only become suspicious of the tasks he was being ordered to complete in October, when his handlers ordered the laptop to be dropped near the apartment complex.

"D'iu gradually began to understand he was doing something bad and that his actions were illegal," the affidavit stated.

At this point, he allegedly asked the Telegram contacts who he was working for, to which they replied "the Motherland," and the company he was surveilling was involved in providing weapons to Ukraine, resulting in D’iu suspecting the Russian government.

Wong said in the affidavit: "Based on my training, experience, and research, D'iu's communications with his Telegram contacts is consistent with the tactics of [Russian intelligence] and its criminal proxies for spotting, assessing, recruiting, and handling intelligence assets and sources. 

"D'iu's targeting of the company and its employees is also consistent with [Russian intelligence] objectives in Russia's war against Ukraine."

The Russian national was indicted and charged with two counts related to spying offences, and one count related to the fake identity documents. He is next due in court on November 24 but remains in federal custody. ®

data.title: Europe's biggest gas supplier battling cyberattack – with no timeline for recovery
data.description:
Norwegian energy giant Equinor is battling a cyberattack on its IT systems, though the company insists that hackers haven't disrupted its oil and gas production.

Equinor, Europe's largest supplier of natural gas, first disclosed the attack on Tuesday evening, saying it had called in the relevant resources to deal with the intrusion and had found no indication that any data had been stolen.

In an update on Wednesday, the company said it had a better handle on how the attack was carried out and which of its systems had been compromised, though it stopped short of sharing either of those details.

"As this is not a virus attack, there is no risk of the attack spreading," Equinor said. The company added that it had found nothing to suggest the incident would affect employees, partners, or suppliers.

In a further update on Thursday, Equinor said the attack remained ongoing but did not appear to be specifically targeting the company. Production continued normally, with no indications that data had been stolen or altered. The incident has been reported to police.

What kind of attack Equinor is dealing with remains a mystery. The company hasn't identified those responsible, disclosed whether it's received any demands from the hackers, or said when it expects the affected systems to be fully restored.

The Register has asked Equinor to elaborate, including whether any of its UK operations have been affected and whether the hackers managed to venture beyond its corporate IT network.

Equinor spokesperson Ellen Maria Skjelsbæk told Norwegian news agency NTB that the company hadn't lost access to its IT systems, though staff could have trouble accessing some corporate applications and services. Email appears to be among the casualties, with Reuters reporting that the company's internal email system was down.

Equinor, which traded as Statoil until 2018, is still largely in the hands of the Norwegian state, which owns 67 percent of the company. The oil and gas biz employs around 25,000 people and operates in more than 20 countries.

The bulk of Equinor's oil and gas production takes place off the coast of Norway, but the company also pumps oil and gas in the UK, US, Brazil, and Canada. It's one of the companies behind Dogger Bank, the enormous offshore wind project off England's northeast coast, and is also in the business of capturing and storing carbon dioxide.

Equinor's assurances about production will be particularly welcome in Europe, which has become increasingly reliant on Norwegian gas since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

The attack comes just weeks after Norway's National Security Authority (NSM) raised its cyberattack risk assessment to four on a five-point scale. The agency said the number of successful cyber operations against Norwegian businesses had tripled over the preceding six months and warned of potential disruption to essential services, including water and electricity supplies.

Europe has already had a few nasty reminders this year of what happens when hackers get their hands on industrial equipment. Last week, the French government pinned a series of cyberattacks targeting refrigeration systems at more than 700 retail sites in October on a hacking unit affiliated with Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. The crooks turned up the temperature in supermarket fridges and freezers, ruining tens of millions of euros' worth of food and starting fires at some premises.

Nothing suggests Equinor's hackers have similar ambitions, or that they've got anywhere near the kit used to extract and transport oil and gas. Given how much of Europe depends on that kit continuing to work, a little more detail from the Norwegian energy giant wouldn't go amiss. ®

data.title: Chase, Visa, Mastercard confirm third-party cyberattacks that may have exposed customers' info
data.description:
JPMorgan Chase, Visa, and Mastercard have all confirmed that they are investigating third-party breaches that may involve customer information after a data-theft-and-extortion gang claimed to have compromised the financial giants.

“Visa is aware of these claims,” a spokesperson told The Register on Thursday. “They are associated with an incident involving a third-party service provider in Asia Pacific. Visa’s systems were not involved and were not impacted. No payments data such as card numbers were affected. This is unrelated to any of the system disruptions across different industries this past week.”

Mastercard also cited a third-party provider in an email sent to The Register following our questions about the alleged breach.

“We were recently informed of an incident at a third-party provider that resulted in the exposure of a limited amount of email addresses - non-payments information - from a small subset of cardholders enrolled in a specific benefit program,” Mastercard SVP Seth Eisen said. “There is no impact to the Mastercard payment network or the ability for people to use their cards. At this time, the exposure has been contained and our teams are working with the provider to support the impacted cardholders as needed.”

JPMorgan Chase did not respond to The Register’s request for comment, but confirmed it was investigating a cyberattack on social media.

“We have learned that third parties who provide services to the firm were the target of a cyber attack,” America’s largest bank posted on X. “Based on our investigation so far, we believe the attackers accessed certain marketing data held by those vendors, which may include some customer names and email addresses.”

According to Chase, the third-party breach didn’t disrupt any of its services, and it’s not connected to the outages earlier in the week attributed to a software bug in on-premise hardware systems.

“There is no connection to service disruption some customers experienced earlier this week,” the bank said on Thursday.

None of the three financial firms would comment on who the third-party providers are, when the breaches occurred, and what specific data was stolen. The Register will update this story as we learn more details about the intrusions.

Extortion crew n0n claimed responsibility for all three alleged hacks, posting the financial giants to its data-leak site on Monday. The group, believed to be based in Russia, emerged in September and posted 108 victims over its first month in operations. ®

data.title: Flaws in VMware and KVM need attention, if you have time while fixing Java, PHP, and everything else
data.description:
If you’ve got a moment to spare in between sorting out emergency patches for PHP, Java, and PostgreSQL, VMware has just bid for any remaining space on your schedule by publishing two critical-rated security advisories.

VMSA-2026-0009 addresses CVE-2026-123890, a 9.8-rated flaw that VMware says means a malicious actor with network access to vCenter may exploit this issue to bypass authentication and gain unauthorized access to the system. vCenter is the tool admins use to manage fleets of virtual machines. The flaw is present in VMware’s flagship Cloud Foundation suite. 

VMware also wants its users to address CVE-2026-123891, which allows attackers to read and write the database used by SDDC Manager, the tool for managing entire software-defined datacenters. Attackers can execute arbitrary commands and elevate privileges to root.

The prospect of an unknown party getting access to vCenter or SDDC manager is not pleasant. At least VMware has fixed its software.

The virty giant hasn't done the same to address a second advisory, VMSA-2026-0010, which warns that Cloud Foundation, Aria Operations, and VCF Operations HCX products all use Apache – which has a 9.8-rated remote code execution vulnerability (CVE-2026-119618).

VMware plans to ship new versions of its products with a patched version of Apache, but for now only has workarounds that disable the http2 protocol.

A KVM curiosity

Admins who oversee virtual infrastructure also need to pay attention to Linux KVM, the subject of a curious incident over the last 24 hours.

This mess started with the November 18 disclosure of CVE-2026-99312, a bug which allows an attacker to use a guest virtual machine to inflict Denial of Service (DoS) or memory corruption attacks on the host.

It’s bad news whenever someone with access to a guest VM can attack the host, because it means gaining access to a single tenant can potentially harm all the other guest VMs or peer into the memory a guest uses.

This flaw, however, isn’t a worst-case scenario guest-host escape, because it only impacts users of AMD processors who employ nested virtualization – the practice of running a hypervisor inside a virtual machine. Nested virtualization isn’t commonly used in the enterprise, but clouds employ it to do things like powering OS emulators. The bug’s CVSSv3 score is therefore a modest 5.5.

Security researcher Oren Tomtov of Accomplish.ai says the flaw meant he could access 127 GB of host RAM on a Digital Ocean “Droplet” – the junior cloud’s name for its cloudy VMs.

Yomtov says he told Digital Ocean and the Linux kernel security team about the flaw in October. Maintainers got busy and delivered a fix to the mainline kernel on November 2, full fixes landed on the 17th. The CVE then appeared on November 18.

Yomtov and Terra Security quickly posted their analysis of the flaw – but then took the posts down within hours.

The Register understands that Digital Ocean asked for the posts to come down because it needed more time to update its Linux implementations. The company has not responded to multiple requests for comment.

Terra’s analysis of the flaw asserts that it was introduced to KVM in 2022, when developers wrote a fix for CVE-2022-3344. The company believes 3.2 percent of CVEs in the Linux kernel were introduced by the fix for another CVE.

The good news about CVE-2026-99312 is it’s easy to defeat without an update, by disabling nested virtualization in KVM. ®

data.title: Palo Alto Networks opens wallet for open-weight training biz
data.description:
As AI has become a thorn in the side of the security industry, Palo Alto Networks (PAN) has reached an agreement to acquire Applied Compute, an AI model training platform.

"We believe many of the major disruptions of the last few weeks, including outages across major enterprises and governments, were partially due to unintended consequences of patching and configuration changes, as IT teams simply cannot patch these vulnerabilities fast enough without compromising their production environments," said Nikesh Arora, chairman and CEO of PAN, during the company's fiscal Q1 2027 earnings call on Wednesday. "The second effect is the rise of AI-assisted cyberattacks."

So in the spirit of "hair of the dog that bit me," PAN is ingesting Applied Compute to make open-weight AI more secure for corporate customers. The answer to insecurity brought on by AI is buying security with AI.

In its announcement of the tie-up, PAN declares "the future of enterprise AI is hybrid, and that a large share of enterprises will run on open-source and open-weight models tuned to their own data, cost, and control needs."

That view has been clouded a bit by Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang's fall from grace: Back in July, he came to the defense of open-weight models as a defense against the hegemony of purveyors of closed-weight commercial models like Anthropic, Google, Microsoft, and OpenAI. His resignation as CEO of Nvidia has led to worries that the open-weight ecosystem has lost some lobbying power at a time when the US is wary about the uptake of models made in China.

Nonetheless, PAN clearly sees a future for open-weight models.

"Every enterprise is going to run a mix of open and closed models, and every one of those models needs to be secured," said Nikesh Arora, chairman and CEO of PAN, in a statement. "Applied Compute has built the best post-training and inference platform we've seen, and its research team is exceptional."

The company expects the $4.5 billion all-stock transaction to add more than $1 billion to the company's Next Generation Security business by FY 2029. 

Arora, on the company's earnings call, explained the pricey bet as recognition of the corporate desire to avoid vendor lock-in and to retain control of data.

"We're already seeing the desire for sovereignty and control compel enterprises to adopt open-weight and open-source models," he said. "Early signs of that shift are clear, with open-weight models growing from under 5 percent of token traffic to more than 60 percent over the past year."

Beyond the sticker price, PAN is ready to up its infrastructure ante. Arora said the biz expects to build infrastructure supporting more than 100 megawatts of inference capacity, a project that will take "a modest CapEx commitment of less than $3 billion through fiscal 2030." ®

data.title: Germ Network infects Android, but in a good way
data.description:
The Germ Network encrypted messaging client, known as Germ DM, became available for Android on Wednesday, and made a bigger splash than its iOS touchdown back in 2023.

"Our usage took a 20x jump yesterday from our Android launch," co-founder Tessa Brown, a communications scholar and former Stanford lecturer, told The Register in an interview. "Android has been really exciting for us because not only is it 70 percent of the global mobile market, but we rolled out on iOS first. People were so excited to use Germ for their end-to-end encrypted Bluesky DMs, but half of their friends couldn't talk to them."

Building a new messaging platform isn't easy, much less one with credible end-to-end encryption. Co-founder Mark Xue hails from Apple, where he worked as a privacy engineer on systems like iMessage and FaceTime.

"At the core level, the end-to-end encryption is built on a standardized encryption and Messaging Layer Security," Xue said. "The premise of Messaging Layer Security was to be as good as Signal and deployable by many, many different parties in different applications, which we're taking advantage of to extend the reach of that encryption."

Xue said the app is built with its own transport protocol to minimize the amount of message metadata, adding that while the team hasn't gotten around to a formal security audit, it's a step they're considering.

Germ Network's goal, said Brown, is to give people more confidence when they communicate. "We do that by giving you more tools to protect your identity, to control what you're sharing with whom," she explained.

Instead of using a person's phone number as an identity key, Germ allows users to create cards which represent distinct identities on the network.

"Instead of sharing your number, you share a card," Brown explained. "You can build multiple cards; they're not mutually discoverable. And our vision for the product that will continue shipping over the coming years is that these cards become a more intelligent way to manage your social life, even your work life."

At some point, AI might play a role in that, but both Xue and Brown expressed reservations about the current state of play.

Citing concerns Signal has raised about the integration of AI and messaging, Xue said, "The products today that I might characterize as technology demos, they're most powerful when they run on someone else's computer. So you end up with these systems where you upload all your messages or you give another entity the power to observe your computing, and that's extremely dangerous for what we protect as private content."

Xue noted rapid progress toward addressing information exposure concerns and therefore plans to explore the kinds of smart tooling that users want while also meeting security and privacy requirements.

"I think a lot of the AI conversation sometimes is a hammer in search of a nail," said Brown. "But people do want more tools to make sense of their busy lives and following our consumers, our users, and what they want, we do want to give them smart tooling that will help them organize threads, stay in touch, find the right people to talk to in groups, in a private way that's using a lot of the intelligence that's already on their device."

If Germ DM were simply trying to win people away from widely adopted services like Instagram or respected encryption apps like Signal, it would be difficult to see a path to success.

But Germ DM may be able to reach a point of sustainability by standing on the shoulders of Bluesky.

Bluesky launched Direct Messages in 2024 but chose to focus its development resources elsewhere and left E2E DMs to Germ Network. Germ DM, which supports Bluesky's AT Protocol (ATproto), fills that gap and even has Bluesky promoting the app for that purpose. 

"On a business strategic level, it's been a really wonderful move for us," said Brown. "So we're natively a multi-identity messenger. And you can say that ATproto is the first external identity that we brought into the app, after we first shipped local identities that you just build in our app.

"And so the way that we're marketing and growing right now is [by offering] end-to-end encrypted messages for Bluesky users. You log in with your handle into our app. We pull your friend graph so you can see your mutuals that already have Germ in the app."

Bluesky assists further with marketing by allowing Germ DM users to add a Germ messaging button to their Bluesky profiles. So anyone interested in encrypted DMs in Bluesky may end up seeing that option.

At some point, expect paid, premium features but at the moment, Germ Network is focused on spreading the encrypted word. ®

data.title: Anthropic throws open doors at $2T valuation as shares pop 34% in initial trading
data.description:
Welcome to the world of public AI frontier labs: Anthropic is now a publicly-held company with its Thursday IPO, and investors are clamoring for a piece of the pie, for now anyway.

That $83 IPO price didn’t last long, with shares rocketing to $111.50 by the time the public could get their hands on them at the end of the initial auction. That means that the company was valued at around $2 trillion as of the public availability of the 980 million shares it put up for sale, a 34 percent increase over the IPO price. 

At just under six years old, Anthropic’s meteoric rise to that valuation has sent investors into a frenzy despite uncertainties surrounding the company’s future profitability. As we’ve noted, Anthropic is on the hook for nearly $1 trillion in compute obligations that could drag its profitability prospects down if any one of a number of scenarios happens to materialize. 

Amodei was on hand to address some of those questions with CNBC this morning following the opening of markets on his company’s big day. 

When asked about the risk Anthropic’s massive compute bills to its bottom line, Amodei admitted the company’s needs are difficult to predict, and that - get this - they try to err on the low side. 

That’s right: The $900 billion in infrastructure and compute commitments that Anthropic revealed in a recent regulatory filing, which could end up surpassing $1T in short order, might just be an underestimate of what the company will need in coming months and years. 

Not to worry, though, the Anthropic CEO insisted: It’s worth it. 

“We’re willing to put into place these very large compute spends because, historically, we’ve seen that it pays off,” Amodei told CNBC’s Ross Sorkin, adding that the returns on the cognitive capabilities of its new models are “so high” as to make all that spending worth it - eventually, one would assume based on his comments, Anthropic is sure to come out on top. 

But what of the threat of open models that could undermine the constant push at Anthropic and other frontier labs to create the most power-hungry, resource-intensive, and powerful AI? Bah, that’s not a problem either. 

Frontier model makers like Anthropic, Amodei said, have already proven that they can do the heavy lifting at the bleeding edge, so you can trust it to make reliable models that are cheaper and less capable, too. 

“Anthropic can compete both at and away from the frontier,” The Anthropic CEO said. 

Whether that’ll mean long-term success for investors is another thing altogether. Mozilla president Mark Surman doesn’t think valuation translates into long-term success, for one. He told The Register this morning that the one thing he consistently hears from developers is that they want AI they can control, not rent from a frontier lab. As Amodei suggested in his comments, Anthropic is aware that those with less intense AI needs might not choose its models, and that could harm the company. 

“Pushing AI toward open source matters so much right now,” Surman said in an email. “Mozilla’s own research this year found that open source models account for a third of all tokens, while the gap with the best closed models is down to about 3.3 per cent.”

In other words, keep an eye on that Anthropic stock - it might be hot now, but reality could still catch up to the company with the biggest-ever IPO.

“The market is already moving,” Surman said. “No valuation changes that.” ®
